Not vaccinated -- no job

By: Eugene Botha | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...can an employer fire an employee for refusing to be vaccinated

Unique Selling Point:
This is a topic that affects all of us in South Africa at the moment

Summary:
With Covid-19 the spectre of forced vaccinations has raised its head. Two recent CCMA rulings found in favour of employers who fired workers for not being vaccinated. But the CCMA is not a court of law -- what exactly is the legal position of people who refuse to be vaccinated. And does Omicron make a difference? What does the Constitution say about all of this?

Further information:
NOT VACCINATED, NO JOB!
This is something many South Africans who are not vaccinated for many reasons are now faced with. The CCMA case involving Theresa Mulderij is a case in point.

The CCMA found in favour of the previous employer, Goldrush, who fired her because she refused to be vaccinated.

She took them to task at the CCMA and the commissioner Lungile Mashake ruled against her, saying she was “permanently unfit for work” because she is not vaccinated.

This ruling was quite controversial – and many people who have been reluctant to vaccinate now fear repercussions from their employers, are now fearing that they too will lose their jobs.

On the 1st of February there was another ruling by the CCMA that again found in favour of an employer who fired and employee for refusing to vaccinate.

I think it is time for us to investigate the legal aspects around this and what it all means, especially since this is not a precedent setting case (unlike High Court Judgments) and the ruling can be challenged in the labour court. Mulderij is planning to do this.

Many people vaccinated and unvaccinated currently want to know what the legal position is regarding employers rights to act against employees who do not want to vaccinate.

It is question raised in South Africa by many people and it is highly relevant.

International trends
In the USA the Biden administration gave orders that all employees working are large companies and firms must be vaccinated. However, this was challenged in the Supreme Court and the court ruled that people cannot be forced to vaccinate.

At the same time the UK has dropped all Covid restrictions and even Denmark is in the process to declare Covidn-19 an endemic virus and is not designating it any longer as a “societally critical” disease. This would also means that vaccinations would be completely discretional like the annual flu jab.

Back home
The uncertainty persists and it seems that the higher Courts and perhaps even the Constitutional Court should rule on this, so that there is clarity.

An additional layer is the medical information that vaccinations are actually not effective against the spreading of the virus – at most it can make an illness less severe. So vaccinated people are to some extent protected against severe illness, but that is all. Unvaccinated people spread the virus at the same rate as vaccinated people. The only different is that vaccinated people have less of a risk of severe symptoms. So, it is the unvaccinated that are at risk in a work setting, more than the vaccinated, the argument goes.

On both sides there are strong, emotional arguments and it is causing a rift between people, and even in families in many instances.
Perhaps we should take a look at where all this is heading and what the actual legal position is today.

Potential interviewees

Case studies:
• Theresa Mulderij
• Goldrush
• Gideon Kok, a security officer
• Ndaka Security Services


Experts:
• Independent legal expert - prof Llewellyn Curlewis
• Constitutional lawyer - Pierre de Vos
• Vaccination scientist/expert on Covid developments -- Prof Madi
• Labour lawyers

NB: This story will focus on vaccinations mandates in the workplace and not on other mandates such as vaccinations requirements for travel, etc.

Script:


V/O:
Gideon Kok is an angry and disappointed man. The documents on his table tell the tale of an intense battle with his now former employer. At its heart: a mandatory vaccination policy that Gideon refused to submit to.
Gideon:
This is my body. This is my body. It does not belong to the government; it does not belong to them. I make decisions for my body.
V/O:
Gideon lives in the Vaal Triangle, south of Jo’burg, and had been working for a security company contracted to energy and chemical giant, Sasol. The company’s workplace vaccine policy came into effect in October last year, and while Gideon refused to get the jab, he was initially allowed to have regular PCR tests instead. But, three weeks later, he was told he was no longer welcome. Feeling unfairly treated, he turned to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration but lost his case.
LINK:
Gideon’s case is one of two landmark rulings by the CCMA the past few weeks that sparked an intense debate around mandatory vaccinations and the right of employers to retrench employees who refuse to be vaccinated.
V/O:
In both cases the employers won.
LINK:
And this has put the cat among the pigeons. Not only is the public divided on the issue, but legal experts and labour lawyers also seem to be polarized.
V/O:
Many labour lawyers say the CCMA got it right, but others Like Pearl Kupe say the rulings don’t reflect what we know about the virus – particularly Omicron.
Pearl:
Vaccinated people can contract and transmit Covid just as well as unvaccinated. So, if you are going to dismiss unvaccinated employees because they can transmit and contract Covid then you need to dismiss equally those who were vaccinated in terms of equity and non-discrimination.
V/O:
It’s widely accepted that vaccinated people can still catch Omicron and infect others, and several studies such as this one from the University of Copenhagen found the same.

So, if vaccines don’t stop the spread of the virus, why insist on a mandatory workplace policy?

Well, because the science is complex and, according to WITS Vaccinology Professor, Shabir Madhi, vaccines still offer significant benefits.
Madhi:
People that are vaccinated, firstly the are less likely to be infected, and they are less likely to transmit the virus. Even with Omicron, people who are vaccinated, they shed the live virus for a shorter period of time which means that even though they might start with as high a viral load as an unvaccinated person, the duration of time that that they will be infectious will probably be less than an unvaccinated individual.
V/O:
In other words, unvaccinated employees still pose a greater threat than their vaccinated colleagues because they’re infectious for longer and risk exposing the immunocompromised and elderly, in particular, to severe disease.

But what of emerging evidence suggesting Omicron is much less severe than earlier strains of the virus? Death rates are down in many parts of the globe but the World Health Organization maintains the virus is still hospitalising and – in some cases killing – many of the people it infects.

For example, recent South African stats show Omicron was still claiming lives.
Madhi:
When we see who ends up in hospital, it is unvaccinated people. Who ends up dying? 85% of people that end up in hospital that are dying in South Africa are unvaccinated or inadequately vaccinated.
V/O:
Thvere disease altered the rationale for vaccination. The initial clinical trials tested against earlier strains, showed the jabs were up to 95% effective at preventing symptomatic infection. Then came Omicron, and that figure plummeted to around 50 % - even less for some vaccines.
Madhi:
We have seen in our data that it is no longer about protecting against infection, but about protecting against severe disease and death. We need to do everything that is possible in that work environment to ensure the safety of everybody in that work environment, rather the prioritizing the preferences of a single individual. And the best way to achieve this is to get everyone vaccinated.
V/O:
Despite its complexity – and controversy – in June last year new Occupational Health and Safety directives were introduced allowing for mandatory vaccinations. They came months before the arrival of Omicron.
LINK:
The amended regulations published by Government in last year do not compel an employer to impose mandatory vaccination, but it merely makes an allowance for mandatory vaccination should an employer feel that is the correct approach.
V/O:
And it seems many employers feel it is.

Gerhard Kriel was head hunted as the CEO of a prominent agricultural organisation.
Gerhard:
I was found to be the best candidate and an appointment was made during December and I started working the beginning of January2022.
V/O:
But after just three weeks the chairman of the board called him to a guest house and told him the company had a mandatory vaccination policy, and that he had to comply.
Gerhard:
So we had a discussion the Thursday evening at the guest house and I was told to make a decision by the next day whether I am going to get vaccinated or not, and the next day the Chairman said “Ok, it is Friday, this is a quick discussion that you should be having with your wife, these discussion do not take long, so by Saturday you need to call me and tell me what your decision is.
V/O:
He refused. (PAUSE) And just two weeks later he was barred from his office, and then suspended. Refusing to walk away, he’s taking the company to court.

Gerhard is arguing that his constitutional rights have been violated – and opinion he shares with many others hot under the collar about mandates.
Pearl:
This is not about mandatory vaccination, Mac. This is about constitutional rights. Your freedom of association, your freedom of movement, your freedom of speech, freedom of religion, belief, and opinion. These are constitutionally entrenched rights. Your right of freedom to choose and right to decide what goes into your body. These are constitutional freedoms, and this is what the fight is about.
V/O:
And across the globe, people who feel their rights are being trampled are taking the fight to their governments, with protests erupting in countries as far afield as Canada and New Zealand. When the American government tried to make vaccination compulsory for employees of larger companies, the supreme court ruled against it.

Here, the debate around mandatory vaccinations is just as fierce and divisive. Towards the middle of last month, students at several universities protested against planned mandates at their campuses. Many, such as those making their voices heard at the University of the Free State, were arrested.
LINK:
In this whole debate the Constitution seems to feature quite prominently, but to get some clarity on this matter, we decided to come to Cape Town to speak to a Constitutional law expert.

V/O:
That’s Professor Pierre de Vos, who lectures at the University of Cape Town. He argues that even fundamental Constitutional rights such as bodily integrity and freedom of choice aren’t absolute and can be limited at times.
De Vos:
You balance different interests. My individual personal interest versus the interest and safety of and the health of the society.

Mac:
You see that is where the conundrum is because what are the principles around that?

De Vos:
It is all about proportionality. So, the more important the purpose of vaccination is -- saving lives, reducing the spread and whatever -- the more likely it is that the court will say it is proportionate to actually impose a vaccine mandate.
V/O:
It’s a view shared by the Human Rights Commission. Towards the end of last year, it said “…it would be constitutionally permissible to require people to vaccinate...”

But uncertainty remains: both the constitutionality of the government approved mandates and the CCMA rulings haven’t been tested in court. And with both sides in the debate standing their ground, it’s likely the country’s highest court will have the ultimate say.
De Vos
It will be surprising if one of these cases do not get all the way to the Constitutional Court… The court will weigh up the interests, but they will rely on the verifiable medical evidence and will not rely on Facebook posts that has nothing to do with actual medical evidence.
V/O:
And that evidence will have to cover all the medical objections to mandatory vaccines, including claims that they have the potential to cause harm.
Mac:
Prof there are many people that fear the detrimental side effects of being vaccinated. Are these fears ungrounded, because these fears are people’s reality.

Madhi:
There are some side effects, and there are some fatal side effects, but the magnitude of that is in the region of maybe say one in 250 000, one in a million. At the worst-case scenario.
LINK:
The controversy around mandatory vaccinations in the workplace is raging on in South Africa at the moment, and only the courts will be able to clarify matters.
V/O:
And while that will end the legal uncertainty around mandatory vaccinations, the futures of those who refuse the jab are anything but. People like Gideon who - rightly or wrongly – took a stand and now bear the consequences.
Gideon:
I would be able to still survive about, with my current savings, for about 2 months. And that would be about it, I think.

An additional layer is the medical information that vaccinations are actually not effective against the spreading of the virus – at most it can make an illness less severe. So vaccinated people are to some extent protected against severe illness, but that is all. Unvaccinated people spread the virus at the same rate as vaccinated people. The only different is that vaccinated people have less of a risk of severe symptoms. So, it is the unvaccinated that are at risk in a work setting, more than the vaccinated, the argument goes. On both sides there are strong, emotional arguments and it is causing a rift between people, and even in families in many instances. Perhaps we should take a look at where all this is heading and what the actual legal position is today.
